beats.say: Brikby. A Gurugram startup that automates property title checks for Indian lenders. This lecture is about the business first: the problem, what they sell, who pays and why, and how big they are. Then a high level view of the system, two questions to ask, and what to say. Eight short sections, and one check after each.
First, a rule about evidence. Every claim carries one of three labels.
Public. It's on their site, their careers page, or LinkedIn. Say it freely: I read your site.
Observed. What any visitor's browser downloads when it opens their site. You use it only to aim your questions. You never quote it in the room.
Estimate. My arithmetic, or an industry assumption. Fine to say, as long as you call it an estimate.
Section one. The problem they solve. Why does a lender need a title check at all?
A home loan, or a loan against property, which everyone calls LAP, is secured by the property. If the borrower stops paying, the lender's protection is the property.

So before the lender pays out, it must be sure of three things. The borrower really owns the property. The title is clean. And nobody else has a charge on it. If the title is bad, the security is worthless.
Lenders don't check this themselves. Each file goes to an empanelled advocate, or a legal vendor firm. And the advocate does four things.
Reads every property document in the file. Sale deeds, gift deeds, tax receipts, approvals. Often dozens of pages each.
Traces ownership back thirteen or thirty years. The lender's policy sets which.
Checks the government's records for any loan or charge already on the property.
And writes a Title Search Report, or a Legal Scrutiny Report, in that lender's own format. Only then does credit sanction the loan and the money go out.
Why it hurts, in Brikby's own public numbers. Seven to fifteen days per file.
Thirty to forty percent of the reviewer's time goes to reading regional and handwritten records.
And manual review misses things, and opinions differ across vendors and branches.
So who loses if a defect is missed? The lender. The property can't be enforced as security. That's why accuracy matters even more than speed.
Check 1. If a title defect is missed, who carries the loss? A, The borrower. B, The advocate, always. C, The lender: its security can't be enforced. Or D, The registrar's office.
C. The lender. Its security is only as good as the title behind it, which is why it pays for a legal opinion on every single file.
Section two. The workflow Brikby plugs into, and the words you need to speak it.
Here's one loan file. The borrower on the left, the lender at the top, the legal vendor in the middle, what the vendor checks along the bottom, and the report on the right.
Step one. The borrower hands over the property papers and the lender opens the loan file.
Step two. The file goes out to an empanelled advocate or a legal vendor firm. So the vendor's turnaround becomes the lender's turnaround.
Step three, scrutiny. The vendor traces the chain of title, reads the encumbrance certificate, and checks the state's land records.

Step four, queries. Every gap goes back to the borrower. A missing link deed. An EC that stops a few years short. A name spelt one way in the deed and another in the land record. Each round trip adds days.
Step five. The vendor writes the Title Search Report, or Legal Scrutiny Report, in that lender's own format. Seven to fifteen days, end to end.
Step six. Credit reads it, sanctions, and then the money goes out. No clean title, no disbursal.
Now the vocabulary. The chain of title: every transfer from the oldest deed, the mother deed, to today's owner, with no gap.
The EC, the Encumbrance Certificate. The registrar's list of registered sales, mortgages and charges on the property over the search period.
The RoR, the record of rights: who the state's land records show as owner. And mutation, that record updated after a sale. A deed without mutation is a query.
And the red flags. A gap in the EC. A missing deed. A power of attorney sale in the chain. Names that don't match.
Plus approvals: a sanctioned building plan, an occupancy certificate, and RERA registration for projects.

And the core difficulty. Every state keeps its land records its own way, on its own portal, in its own language. The Khatauni in Uttar Pradesh, the seven twelve in Maharashtra, the RTC in Karnataka. Often scanned, often handwritten.
One current fact worth knowing: Telangana's Dharani portal was replaced by Bhu Bharati in April twenty twenty five.
Check 2. The encumbrance certificate covers thirty four of the thirty eight years the policy asks for. Pass, or query?
Query. A charge registered in those four missing years would be invisible, so the vendor asks for a fresh encumbrance certificate that covers the gap.
Section three. What Brikby sells, from their own public pages.
Brikby does instant property ownership verification for banks and NBFCs. You upload a file's documents, any state, any language, handwritten included, and in under thirty minutes you get a report.
Document scrutiny. Each document with its key fields: the parties, dates, survey numbers, registration details.
Title flow. The chain of title, rebuilt across the deeds.
Missing documents, like a deed the EC mentions that nobody supplied. And red flags by severity. High: a missing title document. Medium: a fresh EC needed. Low: a name spelt differently.

Loan type insights, because a home loan, a LAP, a balance transfer and self construction ask different questions. A balance transfer cares about the existing lender's charge being released; self construction cares about the plot and the approved plan. And the report comes out in the customer's own format. Their words: bank format trained, bank policy trained.
And checks against government records, not just the documents the borrower happened to supply. That's what catches the charge nobody mentioned.
Their public numbers. Eighty percent faster. Turnaround from four days to under thirty minutes.
Ninety five percent plus accuracy, claimed.
Fifty plus regional languages.
And fifteen thousand plus loan files since January.
They're a twenty twenty five company in Gurugram, and the plan is: become the standard in banking and financial services, then ownership verification for any use case.
The founders, both public. Rishabh Agarwal, the CEO, ex Savills, in real estate valuations. He knows the property and lender side.
Sahith Desham, the CTO, ex UBS, a data engineer. Expect him to care about pipelines, and how you know the output is right.
So, the property side and the data side.
If you remember one sentence, make it this. Brikby replaces days of an advocate's manual title check with an AI drafted report in under thirty minutes, that the lawyer or the credit team reviews.
Check 3. Name three things in a Brikby report.
Any three of these. Document scrutiny. The title flow. Missing documents. Red flags by severity. Loan type insights. The customer's own format. And checks against government records.
Section four. The business. Who pays, why they pay, and what the moat is.
The customers. Lenders' legal and credit teams, at banks, NBFCs and housing finance companies. And the legal vendor firms they empanel.
Pricing, publicly. Report credits, shared by an organisation. The self serve list price is two hundred rupees a report. Enterprise deals are presumably negotiated, but that's an estimate.

Why they pay. Faster disbursal wins borrowers: in lending, the lender that sanctions first often gets the loan. Fewer people per file. The same quality across every vendor and branch, instead of opinions that differ. And month end peaks handled, when every lender rushes to close its numbers and the advocates are buried.
And the moat. Not the model. The long tail. Every state's documents and portals, every lender's format and policy, and the eval data that proves accuracy on them.
What it replaces is advocate time, a few thousand rupees per file, as an estimate. So at two hundred rupees a report, the saving is obvious, and the real sale is speed and consistency.
Know the competitors, briefly. TEAL, API due diligence for lenders.
Landeed, AI title reports.
Square Yards, property data and risk.
If they ask how Brikby is different, the honest answer from their own pages is the lender's own format and policy, and the handwritten, regional long tail.
The value line. The vendor's turnaround is the lender's disbursal time, and a missed defect is the lender's loss. So Brikby sells speed, without giving up a defensible legal opinion.
And why the customer's own format matters: lenders won't change their report format for a vendor. Matching it is what makes adoption easy.

Check 4. Why does "bank format-trained" matter commercially? A, It reduces the OCR cost. B, Lenders won't change their format for a vendor, so matching it makes adoption easy. C, It's an RBI requirement. Or D, It makes the model more accurate.
B. Lenders won't change their report format for a vendor. Producing each lender's own format means they can adopt it without changing how they work.
Section five. How big are they, roughly? These are all estimates, from their public fifteen thousand files.
Fifteen thousand files since January is about fourteen hundred files a month.
About sixty five a working day. And month end in lending is real, so two to three times that on a peak day.
A file has about thirteen documents and seventy pages. So thousands of pages a day.
And only five to eight files in flight at a busy hour. Two hundred files over a ten hour peak day is twenty an hour, and each takes well under thirty minutes.
All estimates. Say roughly. And if they correct you with real numbers, that's a win: you've started a conversation about their system.

So here's the point to make. At this size, throughput is easy. The hard problems are correctness on messy documents, slow and flaky government portals, cost per file, and auditability: every flag traceable to a page, because a lawyer signs the opinion.
Check 5. At their size, is throughput the hard problem? If not, what is?
No. A few thousand pages a day is small. The hard parts are correctness on messy documents, slow portals, cost per file, and auditability.
Section six. The infrastructure, at a high level. First what it looks like from outside, then how I'd expect the pipeline to work.

This is observed, so in the room you say only one thing: it looks like Firebase and GCP from the outside. Here's the shape. A web app in the browser, cloud storage, serverless API functions, a job record, and the analysis pipeline nobody outside can see.
Upload. The documents go from the browser straight into cloud storage.
Start. The browser asks an API function to start the analysis. It records a job and answers at once. An analysis is a job, not a thirty minute request.
Behind it, the pipeline runs. None of that is visible, so the next board is inference.
Live status. The pipeline updates the job's stage, and the browser is pushed each change. No polling.
And afterwards, the user can edit the report, and payment is in report credits.
Now how I'd expect the pipeline to work. This is an estimate. Draw it in the room as, here's how I'd build it.
Each file is a job on a queue. Every page goes through OCR or a vision model, in parallel.
Classify each document. Is it a sale deed, an EC, a land record, a plan? Then extract its fields, each with a page reference.
Then code takes over. It joins the deeds into a title chain, and applies the lender's policy, the state's rules and the loan type.
Then the government portal checks: the land records, the EC, RERA. These are the slowest and least reliable step, so each one is isolated.
And finally one report JSON with the flags, rendered in each lender's format.
Five design points to go with it, one line each.
The LLM reads, code decides. Models turn messy pages into fields. Code builds the chain and applies policy, because that must be exact and explainable.
Every flag cites its page, so a lawyer can verify it in seconds.
Durable jobs. A queue, retries, idempotency keys so a double click never charges twice, and an outbox so report ready is never lost.
Portals are unreliable. Each one is a separate connector, and a portal that's down marks one check pending instead of blocking the report.
And accuracy is measured. A test set per state and document type, and every lawyer correction becomes a test case.
And the trap. Don't say, I looked at your page scripts.
Say, from outside it looks like a Firebase and GCP stack. Never quote endpoint names, regions, bucket names or customer formats. It sounds like reconnaissance, not curiosity.
Check 6. Why should code, not the LLM, build the title chain and apply lender policy?
Because that part must be exact and explainable. The same file gives the same answer, and every decision traces back to a rule and a page. The model reads; code decides.
Section seven. Two questions to ask them. Both are about the business as much as the system.
Question one. Here's how you'd say it.
How do reports reach your lenders today?
Download, or an integration into their loan system?
And when a lawyer edits a field, which version is the source of truth? Where it leads: one canonical report, delivered by a signed webhook.
Question two.
Where does processing run?
For lender documents, I'd keep storage, OCR, the models and the database in one Indian region.
Which also helps with lenders' security reviews and data residency questions. It's a cost, latency and sales question at once.
And others, if there's time.
Which step produces most of the lawyers' corrections?
Which states are the hardest?
And how do you measure accuracy?
Check 7. Where does question 1 lead, as a design?
To one canonical report on the server, with the lawyer's edits versioned on it, delivered into the lender's system by a signed webhook.
Section eight. What to say. The sixty second answer, your work against their job description, and why this role.
When they ask, what do you know about us, here's the sixty second version.

Lenders can't disburse a home loan or a LAP until a legal vendor confirms the title. Thirteen or thirty years of deeds, the encumbrance certificate, land records, written up in the lender's own format.
That's days of an advocate's time per file, much of it reading regional and handwritten records.
Brikby reads the whole file, rebuilds the chain of title, flags what's missing with severity, checks government records,
and produces the report in the customer's format in under thirty minutes, with fifteen thousand plus files done this year.
At your size, the hard part isn't throughput. It's correctness, slow portals and cost per file. And that's the part I'd want to own.
Now your work, against their job description. Queues, retries and idempotency: DeepLogLens. Kafka, commits after durable writes, and idempotent upserts.
Agents with human approval: the Inventory Ops Agent, LangGraph with approval interrupts.
Traces and evals: DeepLogLens again. An LLM judge, a labelled set, and recall numbers.
Firebase, React, and shipping end to end: InterviewPlanPrep. Firebase Auth and Firestore, React, and two hundred and fifty plus students.
And the thread through all of it: messy input turned into exact, auditable output, asynchronously, with an LLM in the loop. That's their problem too.

And why this role? It's the problem I've been solving. Messy input turned into exact, auditable output, through an async pipeline with an LLM in the loop. But with real lenders depending on it, and I'd own it end to end.
Check 8. Name three things you never say from their page scripts.
Endpoint names, regions, bucket names, and customer formats. At most, it looks like Firebase and GCP from the outside. Good luck. You're ready for this one.
